tasks.description: Define x = 10 globally. Inside a function show_x(), print x. Call the function.
tasks.hint:
Functions can READ global variables without any special keyword — they're visible everywhere.
Define `x = 10` outside any function (at the top level).
Inside `show_x()`: `print(x)` works because Python looks up the enclosing scope.
tasks.walkthrough:
`x` is defined at the top level, so it's global.
Inside `show_x`, Python doesn't find a local `x`, so it looks outward and finds the global one.

tasks.description: Try to modify the global x = 10 inside a function using the 'global' keyword. Print x after calling the function.
tasks.hint:
Without `global x`, assigning inside a function creates a LOCAL variable — the global is untouched.
Add `global x` as the first line of the function to tell Python you mean the global.
Then `x = 20` inside the function changes the actual global.
tasks.solution:
x = 10

def change_x():
    global x
    x = 20

change_x()
print(x)
tasks.walkthrough:
`global x` tells Python that `x` inside this function means the one outside.
Without that line, `x = 20` would create a separate local variable and the print would still show 10.

tasks.description: Create a list of 3 dictionaries, each with 'name' and 'score'. Loop through and print each person's name and score.
tasks.hint:
List of dicts: `people = [{'name': 'Alice', 'score': 90}, ...]`
Loop: `for person in people:` — each `person` is one dict.
Access keys: `person['name']` and `person['score']`
tasks.solution:
people = [
    {'name': 'Alice', 'score': 90},
    {'name': 'Bob', 'score': 75},
    {'name': 'Carol', 'score': 85},
]
for person in people:
    print(f"{person['name']}: {person['score']}")
tasks.walkthrough:
Each item in the list is a dictionary. The loop hands you one at a time as `person`.
The f-string uses double quotes on the outside so the single-quoted keys don't clash.

tasks.description: Given `students = [{'name': 'Alice', 'score': 90}, {'name': 'Bob', 'score': 75}, {'name': 'Carol', 'score': 85}]`, print only students with a score above 80.
tasks.hint:
Loop through the list; for each student check `if student['score'] > 80:`
Inside the if block: `print(student['name'])`
Alice (90 > 80) and Carol (85 > 80) should print; Bob (75) should not.
tasks.walkthrough:
Loop over the records and test the score field of each one.
Only Alice (90) and Carol (85) clear 80, so only their names print.

tasks.description: Given a dict of lists `classes = {'math': [90, 85, 92], 'english': [78, 88, 95]}`, print the average score for each class.
tasks.hint:
Loop: `for subject, scores in classes.items():`
Calculate average: `avg = sum(scores) / len(scores)`
Print: `print(f'{subject}: {avg}')` — format as needed.
tasks.walkthrough:
`.items()` gives each subject name together with its list of scores.
The average is the total divided by the count. `:.1f` keeps the output to one decimal place.

tasks.description: Sort the list `[{'name': 'Bob', 'age': 30}, {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25}, {'name': 'Carol', 'age': 28}]` by age and print the names in order.
tasks.hint:
`sorted(list, key=func)` sorts by whatever the key function returns.
The key should extract the 'age': `key=lambda p: p['age']`
Loop the sorted result: `for p in sorted(...): print(p['name'])`
tasks.walkthrough:
The `key` function is called on each record and its return value is what gets compared.
`lambda p: p['age']` returns the age, so the records are ordered 25, 28, 30.
The loop then prints the name of each record in that order.

lesson.intro:
Two ideas today. Scope is about which variables a function can see. Nested data
is about putting lists inside dictionaries and dictionaries inside lists, which is
how most real-world data actually looks.

sections.heading: Functions can read outside variables
sections.body:
A variable created at the top level of the file is global. Any function can
read it without doing anything special.

sections.heading: But assigning makes a new local one
sections.body:
If a function assigns to a name, Python treats that name as local to the
function. The global is untouched. To change the global on purpose, declare
`global x` at the top of the function. Use this sparingly; passing values in
and returning them out is usually cleaner.
sections.code:
x = 10

def try_change():
    x = 20

def really_change():
    global x
    x = 30

try_change()
print(x)
really_change()
print(x)

sections.heading: A list of dictionaries
sections.body:
Each dictionary is one record, and the list holds many of them. Loop over the
list to get one dictionary at a time, then use keys to reach inside it.

sections.heading: A dictionary of lists
sections.body:
The other way round: each key maps to a list. `.items()` gives you the key
and the list together, and you can run `sum` and `len` on the list.

sections.heading: Sorting records by a field
sections.body:
`sorted()` takes a `key` argument: a function that says what to sort by.
A lambda is a tiny inline function, perfect for "give me the age of this
record". Tomorrow's lesson on lambdas has more.

watch_out: Reading a global then assigning to it in the same function without `global` gives an UnboundLocalError.
Mixing quote types: inside `f"..."` use single quotes for keys, `s['name']`, or the string ends early.
`students[0]['name']` reads left to right: first pick the record, then the field.
Sorting with `key=` doesn't change the original list; `sorted()` returns a new one.
